notes.meaning: God tells Samuel that the time for grieving over Saul's failure is over. Saul has been firmly rejected, and Samuel must fill an animal horn with oil and travel to Bethlehem to Jesse's family. There, God has chosen a new king who will truly lead for Him.

Samuel worries that Saul's unstable anger will lead him to execute the prophet if he learns of a new king being chosen. The Lord gives Samuel a wise plan: take a young cow and offer a public peace offering to the Lord in Bethlehem. Samuel tells the truth about his sacrifice, while keeping the dangerous secret of the anointing quiet for his safety.

Samuel is told to invite Jesse and his household to join in the sacred meal after the offering. God promises to guide Samuel step by step when the family gathers. Samuel is only to pour the oil over the specific son God points out.

Samuel obeys the Lord and arrives in the quiet hill town of Bethlehem. The town elders tremble when they see him, fearing the great prophet has come to punish some secret crime or bring bad news from King Saul. They greet him anxiously to ask whether he arrives with peaceful intentions.

Samuel reassures the elders that his visit brings peace and that he has come to worship God with a sacrifice. He instructs them to wash and prepare their hearts for the holy ceremony. Samuel takes special care to help Jesse and his sons get ready, inviting them to the feast that follows.

When the family gathers, Samuel notices Jesse's oldest son, Eliab. Because Eliab is tall, handsome, and dignified, Samuel assumes at once that this must be the Lord's chosen king. He makes the mistake of judging the man merely by what looks impressive to the eyes.

God gently corrects Samuel by telling him not to be swayed by Eliab's height or good looks, because the Lord has not chosen him. Human beings can only look at outward appearances, but God looks directly at a person's inner character, faith, and motives. True worth before God comes from what is inside a person rather than physical charm.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient Hebrew text is unusually brief here, and they follow the ancient Greek translation to restore phrases about man looking at outward appearance.

notes.meaning: Jesse presents his second son, Abinadab, and then his third son, Shammah, before Samuel. In each case, God gives Samuel an inner sign that neither one is His chosen leader. Samuel faithfully speaks up and tells Jesse that the Lord has chosen neither of them.

Jesse brings four more sons forward, making a total of seven who pass before Samuel. God gives no sign of approval for any of them. Samuel must inform Jesse that the Lord has not chosen a single one of these young men.

Samuel asks Jesse if these are all the sons he has, knowing that God's chosen king must be from this household. Jesse explains that only the youngest is left, out in the fields tending the sheep because the family thought him unimportant. Samuel insists that no one will sit down to eat the feast until the boy is brought in.

Jesse sends for his youngest son, who comes in from the pastures healthy, ruddy, with bright eyes and a handsome look. The moment the youth stands before him, the Lord speaks to Samuel's heart and tells him to rise and anoint him. This ordinary shepherd boy is the king God has selected.

Samuel takes his horn of oil and anoints David in front of his brothers, marking him for God's royal service. At that moment, the Holy Spirit rushes upon David with power to prepare him for his future calling, and Samuel returns home to Ramah. David does not claim the throne right away, but waits patiently for God's timing.

differ.view: The Spirit came upon David not only to equip him for his royal duties, but also to bring true spiritual salvation to his heart.
The Spirit coming upon David in the Old Testament was an empowering for royal leadership and service, rather than the permanent indwelling given to all believers after Pentecost.

notes.meaning: Because of Saul's repeated disobedience, the Holy Spirit withdraws the royal gifts of wisdom and courage that once helped him lead. In their place, a troubling spirit permitted by the Lord afflicts Saul with deep dread and dark moods. When leaders turn away from God, they lose His blessing and open themselves to misery.

differ.view: Saul was never truly saved or inwardly renewed, so the departure of the Spirit shows only that God removed the special gifts of leadership He had granted him for his role as king.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The phrase translated 'evil spirit' can simply mean an injurious or harmful spirit that caused mental distress, rather than an evil demon.

notes.meaning: Saul's royal attendants notice the painful changes in their master's behavior and moods. They recognize that his dark spells are not just an ordinary sickness, but a torment allowed by God as a judgment. They speak honestly to the king about the spiritual trouble that has fallen upon him.

The servants suggest finding someone who can skillfully play the lyre or harp before the king. They believe the soothing sounds of music will calm Saul's troubled spirit and give him relief whenever his dark fits come. Even in ancient times, people recognized that good music can help ease emotional distress.

Saul agrees with the advice of his attendants and welcomes their plan. He commands them to search out a gifted player and bring him to the court without delay. In his deep distress, the king is willing to try anything that might give him peace of mind.

A young attendant reports that he knows one of Jesse's sons from Bethlehem who plays the lyre very well. He praises the young man as brave, sensible in speech, handsome, and clearly blessed with the Lord's presence. God's quiet providence is already at work to bring David into the royal palace.

Saul sends royal messengers to Bethlehem with an order for Jesse to send David, who is still out caring for the sheep. Even after being anointed as future king, David has returned humbly to his ordinary daily work. When the king calls, David is ready to serve.

Jesse packs a customary gift of bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat onto a donkey to show respect to the king. In that culture, coming before a ruler without a gift was considered disrespectful. Jesse sends these gifts along with David as an act of loyal honor.

David arrives at court and enters Saul's personal service. The king takes a great liking to the young man and appoints him as one of his armor-bearers, a position of trust and honor. This gives David valuable firsthand experience in royal court life and military affairs.

Saul is so pleased with David that he sends a message back to Jesse asking permission to keep him at court permanently. Jesse agrees to let his son remain with the king. God continues to give David favor in the eyes of those around him.

Whenever the dark torment from God overtakes Saul, David picks up his lyre and plays before him. The music calms Saul's mind, bringing relief, and the tormenting spirit departs from him for a time. In this way, God's future king acts as a peacemaker and comforter to the troubled ruler.
